summary: For ages 13–14, learners evaluate a contested scientific debate (what drove Pleistocene megafauna extinction — human overkill, climate change, or a combination), interpret what ancient DNA from permafrost can and cannot reveal, connect deep-time extinction to the present-day 'sixth extinction', and construct a reasoned argument about the feasibility AND ethics of de-extinction. The central move is separating the science question ('can we / what caused it?') from the values question ('should we?') and defending a position while acknowledging the other side.
misconceptions: 'Humans alone (or climate alone) caused the megafauna extinctions' — evidence often supports a combination.
'We can clone a mammoth exactly from ancient DNA' — realistically we can only engineer a cold-adapted elephant-hybrid; DNA is degraded and incomplete.
'Ancient DNA can bring back dinosaurs' — DNA degrades over ~thousands to a million years; none survives from 66 My ago.
'De-extinction is obviously good / obviously bad' — it is a genuine dilemma with substantive arguments on both sides.
'A revived species would slot straight back into today's ecosystems' — habitats and ecosystems have changed.

activities.title: In-role debate with a palaeogeneticist (and a conservation ethicist)
steps: Interview a character playing a palaeogeneticist who reads mammoth DNA from permafrost and runs a de-extinction project; begin with the 'whodunit': as humans spread into new continents, many giant mammals vanished — in some regions (e.g., North America) around the time the last Ice Age was ending and warming, but in others (e.g., Australia, roughly 40,000+ years ago) well before that, while Africa lost comparatively few. Ask which was the main driver where, and press for evidence.
Challenge feasibility with concrete questions: 'Is that a real mammoth, or just an elephant gene-edited to be cold-adapted?', 'Why can't you clone it exactly from the DNA you recovered?'
Challenge the ethics: 'What happens to the first calf?', 'Wouldn't that money save species alive today?', 'Who decides whether we do this?'
Optionally stage a second character — a de-extinction advocate versus a conservation ethicist — hear both, then state and defend your own position in your own words.
Answer the turned-back question: 'We may be able to do this soon — tell me, SHOULD we?' State at least one strong argument for and one against, and name what remains uncertain.
activities.insight: A science question ('can we / what caused it?') and an ethics question ('should we?') are distinct; informed people disagree for good reasons; a learner can stake and defend a reasoned position rather than wait to be told the answer.

activities.title: Weigh the evidence: continent timelines of humans, climate and extinction
steps: On a map/timeline per continent, overlay human-arrival dates, climate records for the relevant period (including, but not only, end-of-Ice-Age warming), and the timing of megafauna decline.

Judge where the patterns fit the overkill hypothesis, where they fit the climate hypothesis, and where a combination best explains the data, using a balance meter that weighs overkill vs climate vs combination.
Write a short claim naming, for a chosen continent, which evidence pattern you find most convincing and why, and state what evidence would change your mind.
Use a 'de-extinction toolkit' diagram that lays out the genetic steps and the gaps between them to explain why recovered DNA does not yield an exact clone.
activities.insight: Competing causal hypotheses can be weighed against actual evidence (timing correlations across landmasses), and the data often support interacting causes rather than a single villain.

activities.title: Explore the evidence pieces (introductory scaffold)
steps: Tap a permafrost-preserved mammoth to reveal what ancient DNA can yield (genetics, diet, relatedness) and why it degrades over time.

Tap argument cards to reveal substantive points for and against de-extinction (restore ecosystems, scientific learning, reversing harm vs animal welfare, novel-organism risks, diverting conservation funds, hubris).
After revealing the pieces, close the screen and reconstruct from memory: the two hypotheses, one line of evidence for each, what ancient DNA tells us, and one argument on each side of the ethics.
activities.insight: Orients learners to the key pieces — hypotheses, ancient-DNA limits, and the shape of the ethics debate — as preparation for argument construction.

activities.title: Factual-recall check (use only for the knowledge layer)
steps: Match each line of evidence to the hypothesis it supports (overkill, climate, or consistent with both).
State the two main hypotheses for megafauna extinction (Tier A).
Cite one line of evidence for each hypothesis and explain what ancient DNA can tell us, and why no dinosaur DNA survives (Tier B).

Take the ethics question into the dialogue or a short written argument: construct a reasoned position with at least one strong argument for and one against, and name remaining uncertainty (Tier C) — rather than selecting a single 'right' answer.
activities.insight: Confirms secure recall of the hypotheses, evidence and DNA facts that the evaluative work builds on.

checkQuestion: We have ancient DNA from mammoths frozen in permafrost, and the mammoth went extinct only a few thousand years ago. A company says it can 'bring the mammoth back.' Should we — and could we really recreate an extinct species? Work through what the evidence and the arguments actually support.
checkAnswer: Strong reasoning separates several questions. On WHY they died out: it weighs the overkill (human hunting) and climate (rapid warming) hypotheses using fossil, archaeological and ancient-DNA evidence, and recognises it was likely a combination rather than a single cause. On COULD we: ancient DNA is fragmentary and degraded, so true recreation isn't possible — at best a gene-edited elephant approximation. On SHOULD we: it raises substantive arguments both ways (ecological restoration and lost habitat/behaviour versus animal-welfare, ecosystem-risk, and opportunity-cost against conserving living species), and connects to the present-day sixth mass extinction. It treats these as evidence-and-values questions, not a yes/no fact.
